title: the smallest prayer
hook: forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder: what the hand is tracing
carry: head, heart, shoulders — all of you

segments.voice: A pitcher does it before the first throw. A grandmother does it when the bus passes a church. Someone does it in a hospital hallway, right after the doctor leaves. Forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Two seconds, no words out loud. If you grew up Catholic, your hand may know it better than your head does. It's a prayer, maybe the smallest there is, and the hand is tracing something on purpose.
screen: `A PITCHER. A GRANDMOTHER. A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.` → `TWO SECONDS.` → `THE SMALLEST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: It's old. Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa described believers tracing a tiny cross on their foreheads all day long: getting dressed, sitting down to eat, lighting a lamp. Over the centuries that thumb-sized cross grew into the big one. And it says two things at once. The hand traces the cross, the shape Jesus died on, over your own body. The words name who Catholics believe God is. They come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." One God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That's why many Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door first. Those same words were said over them, with water, at their baptism. Now look where the hand goes. The forehead, where you think. The chest, where your heart is. The shoulders, where you carry things. Many hear it that way: nothing left out. Western Catholics go to the left shoulder first; Orthodox Christians go right, then left. Same sign, two old habits.
screen: `A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD, AROUND 200.` · `THE CROSS, AND THE NAME.` · `HOLY WATER: A REMINDER OF BAPTISM.` · `THINK, FEEL, CARRY.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. If you'd like, make the sign slowly, slower than anyone ever does it: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. Or just rest a hand on each place and notice it. Then let the breath all the way out.
The sign of the cross. The cross traced over all of you, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. First word on your strand.

what a scholar hears: Tertullian, around 200, on crosses traced on the forehead at every step of the day; the larger sign and the shoulder order settled later, differently in East and West.

story.title: sent out, doubts and all
story.text: On a mountain in Galilee, the risen Jesus meets his eleven friends one last time, and the Gospel admits that some of them still doubt. He doesn't wait for them to be sure. He sends them out anyway, to every nation. Go, he says, baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Those are the words Catholics say every time they make the sign.

Tertullian, De Corona 3 (c. 200–211): believers trace the sign on the forehead at every going in and out, dressing, bathing, eating, lighting lamps. Paraphrased and unnamed in the voice ('a Christian writer in North Africa'); confirm the examples chosen.
Western Catholic practice: left shoulder then right; Orthodox: right then left with three fingers joined. Confirm wording.
Holy water as a reminder of baptism ('those same words were said over them, with water'): confirm phrasing.
'Head, heart, shoulders' (think, feel, carry) is a popular reading of the gesture, not a defined teaching; the voice says 'many hear it that way'. Confirm.
Story: Matthew 28:17 says some doubted; the story retells 28:16–20 without quotation marks. Confirm.
